To waffle means to be vague, evasive, or uncommitted — either in what you say or in a decision you make. It always implies a frustrating lack of clarity. The person waffling is dancing around something rather than facing it directly.

There are two closely related flavors of this meaning, shaped largely by geography.
Meaning 1 — Talking a lot but saying very little (mainly British & Australian English)

When someone waffles, they speak or write at great length, using many words, but those words carry very little real substance or meaning. The listener or reader walks away thinking: "What was actually being said there?"

A classic example is a student who doesn't know the answer to an exam question but, rather than leaving it blank, fills half a page with loosely connected, vague sentences, hoping to get some credit. That student is waffling. Similarly, a manager who spends fifteen minutes in a meeting talking in circles without ever making a clear point is waffling.

The key characteristic here is volume without clarity — lots of words, very little content.
Meaning 2 — Being indecisive, going back and forth (mainly American English)

In American English, to waffle means to keep switching between positions or choices without ever committing to one. It describes someone who is wishy-washy, non-committal, or perpetually on the fence.

Imagine a politician asked: "Do you support this policy or not?" They reply: "Well, there are merits on both sides... I see the value in option A, but option B also raises important points... we need to consider all perspectives..." — and never actually answers. That politician is waffling.

The key characteristic here is indecision without resolution — going back and forth without landing anywhere.
How the Two Meanings Connect

Despite the difference, both meanings share one central thread: a frustrating absence of something clear and direct. Whether a person is speaking vaguely for too long, or refusing to commit to a position, the experience for everyone around them is the same — you are left without a satisfying, clear answer or outcome. The person is, essentially, avoiding the point.

This is why both meanings live comfortably under the same word. Waffling, in any form, is the art of saying a lot without committing to anything.
The Tone of the Word

"Waffle" is an informal word. It is also subtly critical — when you say someone is waffling, you are pointing out a flaw in them. You are not being neutral. It implies mild frustration or impatience. You would use it in everyday conversation or informal writing, not in formal reports or official documents.
"Waffle" as a Noun (closely related, worth knowing)

The noun form of waffle (in this context, completely separate from the breakfast food) refers to the actual content produced by waffling. For example: "His speech was pure waffle — I learned nothing from it." This is the British usage, and it describes speech or writing that is empty, vague, and overlong.
Common Ways the Word Is Used

• "Stop waffling and just tell me what you think." — demanding a direct answer
  • "She waffled for ten minutes before admitting she didn't know." — talking vaguely to avoid admitting something
  • "The government keeps waffling on this issue." — refusing to commit to a clear policy
  • "His essay was full of waffle." — the writing lacked substance (noun form)
  • "He waffled between the two job offers for weeks." — unable to make a decision
What Waffling Is NOT

Waffling is not the same as simply being confused or making an honest mistake. It implies an ongoing, extended quality — it stretches over time. Someone who gives one unclear sentence isn't really waffling. And it is not the same as lying — a person who waffles isn't necessarily being dishonest, they are being evasive, unfocused, or indecisive.
A Quick Mental Test

If you ever want to check whether someone is waffling, ask yourself: "After all that, do I have a clear, direct answer?" If they spoke for a long time and you still don't know what they think, intend, or have decided — they were waffling.
Similar Words (to place it in context)

Depending on the situation, waffling can overlap with: rambling (talking without focus), hedging (avoiding commitment to protect yourself), equivocating (using deliberately vague language), and beating around the bush (avoiding the main point). "Waffle" is a bit more informal and colorful than these, and it captures both the volume and the vagueness together quite efficiently.
